$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,3)=-9,\,{f}_{x}(x,y,z)=y,\,{f}_{y}(x,y,z)=x,\,{f}_{z}(x,y,z)=-2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,3),$ estimate the value of $f(0.98,-0.01,3.1).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,0,3)+∇f(1,0,3)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-0,z-3⟩ \\  & =-9+⟨{f}_{x}(1,0,3),{f}_{y}(1,0,3),{f}_{z}(1,0,3)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(1,0,3)$, ${f}_{y}(1,0,3)$ and ${f}_{z}(1,0,3),$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,0,3) & =0 \\ {f}_{y}(1,0,3) & =1 \\ {f}_{z}(1,0,3) & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y,z)≈-9+⟨0,1,-6⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-3⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(0.98,-0.01,3.1)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=0.98,y=-0.01$ and $z=3.1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.98,-0.01,3.1) & ≈-9+⟨0,1,-6⟩\cdot ⟨0.98-1,-0.01,3.1-3⟩ \\  & =-9+⟨0,1,-6⟩\cdot ⟨-0.02,-0.01,0.1⟩ \\  & =-9-0.01-0.6 \\  & =-9.61\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b0b6b4b5-7cfe-50c1-9f11-ac3785660947"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b0b6b4b5-7cfe-50c1-9f11-ac3785660947" :answer-field/id #uuid "b0b6b4b5-7cfe-50c1-9f11-ac3785660947" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c614f0d9-6fb7-53fc-b7ea-7df222acd263" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3d1682a6-0223-5ed8-8277-0f5be1c651f9" "answer-ce98542a-f5c0-51c4-ab6c-242d4d9c6e51" "answer-c614f0d9-6fb7-53fc-b7ea-7df222acd263" "answer-5c547bf0-6a15-5b93-836e-c0f81afbd41f" "answer-d5f80dc7-8dae-5243-9e68-a3715cc5329a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3d1682a6-0223-5ed8-8277-0f5be1c651f9" :answer/id #uuid "3d1682a6-0223-5ed8-8277-0f5be1c651f9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-9.48" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ce98542a-f5c0-51c4-ab6c-242d4d9c6e51" :answer/id #uuid "ce98542a-f5c0-51c4-ab6c-242d4d9c6e51" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-9.55" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c614f0d9-6fb7-53fc-b7ea-7df222acd263" :answer/id #uuid "c614f0d9-6fb7-53fc-b7ea-7df222acd263" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-9.61" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5c547bf0-6a15-5b93-836e-c0f81afbd41f" :answer/id #uuid "5c547bf0-6a15-5b93-836e-c0f81afbd41f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-9.72" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d5f80dc7-8dae-5243-9e68-a3715cc5329a" :answer/id #uuid "d5f80dc7-8dae-5243-9e68-a3715cc5329a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-9.95" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125853 :tutorial/content "Consider the function $f(x,y)=4-x^2-y^2$ at the point $P(1,1).$ We want to find the best linear approximation to this function, valid in a neighborhood of $P.$

The partial derivatives of $f$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =-2x\, & ⟹\, &  & {f}_{x}(1,1)=-2 \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =-2y\, & ⟹\, &  & {f}_{y}(1,1)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

The partial derivatives are continuous functions at every point, which means that $f$ is differentiable everywhere, and

$$
\nabla f (1,1) = \langle -2, -2\rangle.
$$

Therefore, the best linear approximation of $f$ in a neighborhood of $(1,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,1)+∇f(1,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & =2+⟨-2,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & =2+(-2)\cdot (x-1)+(-2)\cdot (y-1) \\  & =2-2x+2-2y+2 \\  & =6-2x-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's take a look at the diagram below. Notice that in the neighborhood of $(x,y)=(1,1)$, the surface and its tangent plane approximation are very close.

![](images/20/20f06226ec7c21583e56249ea2fe5c65c6127cef8a6e05ee4b1d7521ce49dc38.png)

   

Therefore, we can use this to approximate values of $f(x,y)$ that are close to $(1,1).$ For example, using our approximation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.01,1.01) & ≈6-2(1.01)-2(1.01) \\  & =1.96.\end{aligned}
$$

The actual value of $f$ at this point is $1.9598,$ so our approximation is pretty good!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124729 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$
\nabla f (1,1) = \langle -2, -2\rangle.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,1)+∇f(1,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & =2+⟨-2,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & =2+(-2)\cdot (x-1)+(-2)\cdot (y-1) \\  & =2-2x+2-2y+2 \\  & =6-2x-2y.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.01,1.01) & \approx 6-2(1.01)-2(1.01) \\  & =1.96.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(3, -1, 1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(3,-1,1)+∇f(3,-1,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y+1,z-1⟩.\end{aligned}
